title: The Stolen Necklace and the Magic Rooster

full_text:
A wealthy merchant of Cairo hosted a grand banquet for eight of his fellow merchants in his garden pavilion. During the evening, a diamond necklace of immense value, belonging to his daughter, vanished from the dressing table. No stranger had entered the house, and all eight guests vehemently denied taking the jewel.

The merchant summoned the wise Kazi of the city, Abu Masrur, to discover the culprit without falsely accusing an innocent man.

The Kazi placed a black rooster inside a darkened tent in the courtyard. He announced with solemn gravity: 'This is a magical rooster endowed with the power of truth. Each of you eight merchants shall enter the dark tent alone, place his hands firmly upon the back of the rooster, and return. When the guilty man touches the bird, the rooster will crow with a voice like thunder!'

One by one, the eight guests entered the dark tent, stroked the bird, and stepped out into the courtyard. The rooster remained completely silent; not a single crow was heard.

The host cried in despair: 'The magic has failed!'

The Kazi smiled with calm authority: 'The test has not failed; it has just begun! Let all eight gentlemen hold out their hands before me with open palms!'

Seven of the merchants held out hands that were heavily blackened with soot—for the Kazi had coated the rooster’s feathers with wet chimney soot!

The eighth merchant, terrified that the rooster would crow if he touched it, held out hands that were completely clean and white!

Seeing his clean hands, the thief knew he was caught. He fell to his knees in tears, pulled the diamond necklace from his boot, and confessed his crime, proving that guilt creates its own trap through fear, while innocence touches the bird without dread.
moral: Guilt betrays itself through fear, while a clear conscience walks fearlessly in the light.

Believing rumors and flattery without proof
